citation.title: Estimating Average Causal Effects Under General Interference, with Application to a Social Network Experiment

standing_assumptions:
[Population and design: pp. 1914–1915 (PDF pp. 3–4)] Formally, suppose we have a finite population $U$ of units indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, N$ on which a randomized experiment is performed. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, \ldots, z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{1, \ldots, M\}$ specifies which of $M$ possible treatment values that unit $i$ receives. An experimental design contains a plan for randomly selecting a particular value of $\mathbf{z}$ from the $M^N$ different possibilities with predetermined probability $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Restricting our attention only to treatment assignments that can be generated by a given experimental design, define $\Omega = \{\mathbf{z} : p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0\}$ so that $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_N)'$ is a random vector with support $\Omega$ and $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Our analysis below focuses on the case where the design is known in the following sense: $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$ for all $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ is known. [Exposure mapping: p. 1915 (PDF p. 4)] We define an exposure mapping as a function that maps an assignment vector and unit-specific traits to an exposure value: $f : \Omega 	imes \Theta 	o \Delta$, where $	heta_i \in \Theta$ quantifies relevant traits of unit $i$. [Exposures and exposure probabilities: p. 1916 (PDF p. 5)] Define the exposure that unit $i$ receives as $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z}, 	heta_i)$, a random variable with support $\Delta_i \subseteq \Delta$ and for which $\Pr(D_i = d) = \pi_i(d)$. Note that because $|\Delta| \le |\Omega| 	imes N$, $\Delta$ is a finite set of $K \le |\Omega| 	imes N$ values, such that $\Delta = \{d_1, \ldots, d_K\}$. Then for each unit, $i$, we have a vector of probabilities, $(\pi_i(d_1), \ldots, \pi_i(d_K))' =  oldsymbol{\pi}_i$. [...] We have $\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \Omega} \mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \Omega} p_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k)$. [...] we define $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$ as the probability of the joint event that both units $i$ and $j$ are subject to exposure $d_k$, and we define $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$ as the probability of the joint event that units $i$ and $j$ are subject to exposures $d_k$ and $d_l$, respectively. [Probability matrices: p. 1917 (PDF p. 6)] $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_k'$ is an $N 	imes N$ symmetric matrix with individual exposure probabilities, the $\pi_i(d_k)$'s, on the diagonal and joint exposure probabilities, the $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$'s, on the off-diagonals. The nonsymmetric $N 	imes N$ matrix $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_l'$, with zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$, yields all joint probabilities across exposure conditions $k$ and $l$. The zeroes on the diagonal are due to the fact that a unit cannot be subject to multiple exposure conditions at once. [Positivity: p. 1918 (PDF p. 7)] Suppose all units have nonzero probabilities of being subject to each of the $K$ exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for all $i$ and $k$. [Potential outcomes: p. 1918 (PDF p. 7)] In the most general terms, each $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ can generate a potential outcome for unit $i$. We label the randomization potential outcome of unit $i$ associated with $\mathbf{z}$ as $y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$. These randomization potential outcomes are fixed for all units in the population and do not depend on the value of randomized treatment, $\mathbf{Z}$. CONDITION 1 (Properly specified exposure mapping). For all $i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$ and $\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \Omega$ such that $f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = f(\mathbf{z}', 	heta_i)$, $y_i^r(\mathbf{z}) = y_i^r(\mathbf{z}')$. Given Condition 1, each unit $i$ has $|\Delta| = K$ potential outcomes, which we can write in terms of the exposure conditions as $(y_i(d_1), \ldots, y_i(d_K))$, where $y_i(d_k) = y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$, $ orall i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$, $k \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$, and $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ such that $f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k$. Let $Y_i$ be the observed outcome for unit $i$. CONDITION 2 (Consistent potential outcomes). $Y_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) y_i(d_k)$, $ orall i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$. [p. 1919 (PDF p. 8)] Throughout, unless otherwise noted, we will be assuming Conditions 1 and 2. [Estimands: p. 1919 (PDF p. 8)] We seek estimates for all $k$ of $\mu(d_k) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k) =  rac{1}{N} y^T(d_k)$, where $y^T(d_k)$ is the total of the potential outcomes under $d_k$. This allows us to define an average causal effect of being in exposure condition $d_k$ as compared to being in condition $d_l$ as $	au(d_k, d_l) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k) -  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_l)$. [Estimators: pp. 1919–1920 (PDF pp. 8–9)] (1) $\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}$. $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) = (1/N)\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)$, with variance $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)) = (1/N^2)\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$. canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement refuted: p. 1926 (PDF p. 15)] PROPOSITION 6.2. Given Conditions 3, 5, and 6, Wald-type intervals constructed as $\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}$ will tend to cover $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$ at least $100(1 - \alpha)\%$ of the time for large $N$. [Proof step refuted: Appendix A.7, p. 1943 (PDF p. 32)] Denote $a_{ij}(D_i, D_j)$ as the sum of the elements in $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$ that incorporate observations $i$ and $j$. Note that all $a_{ij}(D_i, D_j)$ are bounded above by some finite constant by Condition 3 [...] Thus, $\mathrm{Var}[N\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]] = O(N^{-2} \times N) = O(N^{-1})$. [Counterexample, from the validator] For even $N \ge 4$ put $n = N/2$, $\epsilon_N = N^{-2}$, $q_N = 1/2 - \epsilon_N$ and $t_N = 1 - 2\epsilon_N = 2q_N$. Let $U_N = \{1, \ldots, N\}$, with pairs $(2r - 1, 2r)$, $1 \le r \le n$. Treatment is binary, $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$. The pairs are randomized independently, and within every pair $(a, b)$ $\Pr\{(Z_a, Z_b) = (0, 0)\} = \Pr\{(Z_a, Z_b) = (1, 1)\} = \epsilon_N$ and $\Pr\{(Z_a, Z_b) = (0, 1)\} = \Pr\{(Z_a, Z_b) = (1, 0)\} = q_N$; the probability of a complete assignment is the product of its pair probabilities. Exposure is own assignment, $D_i = Z_i$, with $d_k = 1$ and $d_l = 0$. The potential outcomes are $y_{2r-1}(1) = y_{2r-1}(0) = 1$ and $y_{2r}(1) = y_{2r}(0) = -1$, so $Y_i = y_i(D_i)$ and $\tau(d_k, d_l) = 0$. The populations are nested, outcomes of existing units never change, and the design is reapplied at each $N$, as p. 1924 allows. (a) [The hypotheses hold.] Conditions 1 and 2 hold. $\pi_i(1) = \pi_i(0) = 1/2$ for every unit and $|y_i(d)| = 1$, so Condition 3 holds with $c_1 = 1$, $c_2 = 2$. For distinct units $a, b$ in the same pair, $\pi_{ab}(1) = \pi_{ab}(0) = \epsilon_N$ and $\pi_{ab}(1, 0) = \pi_{ab}(0, 1) = q_N$; for units in different pairs every joint exposure probability equals $1/4$; so every joint exposure probability of two distinct units is positive. With $h_{ij} = 1$ when $i$ and $j$ are in the same pair (including $i = j$) and $h_{ij} = 0$ otherwise, the exposure vectors of any two disjoint sets of units with no $h$-edge between them are independent, and $\sum_j h_{ij} = 2$: Condition 5 holds with $m = 2$ as a genuine dependency graph (the definition corrected as in P013-T6), and also as printed. $\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] = 8t_N/N$, so $N\,\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] = 8(1 - 2/N^2) \to 8$: Condition 6 holds with $c = 8$. (b) [The printed estimator.] Writing $\widehat{V}_N$ for expression (11), $N^2\widehat{V}_N = \sum_{r=1}^{n} R_r$, where for the pair $(a, b) = (2r - 1, 2r)$, $R_r = 2/\epsilon_N$ if $Z_a = Z_b$ and $R_r = 16 - 4/t_N$ if $Z_a \ne Z_b$. $\mathrm{E}[R_r] = 16t_N$, so $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{V}_N] = \mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$ exactly, and every value of $\widehat{V}_N$ is positive. (c) [The variance estimator does not concentrate at or above the true variance.] Let $A_N$ be the event that every pair is split ($Z_a \ne Z_b$ in every pair). Then $\Pr(A_N) = t_N^{N/2}$, $\Pr(A_N^c) \le n \cdot 2\epsilon_N = 1/N$, and on $A_N$, $N\widehat{V}_N = 8 - 2/t_N$. Hence $N\widehat{V}_N \xrightarrow{p} 6$ while $N\,\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] \to 8$, and $\widehat{V}_N/\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] \xrightarrow{p} 3/4$. (d) [The bound of Appendix A.7 fails.] $\mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N) = \frac{4(N-2)^4(N+2)^4}{N^5(N^2-2)}$, which is asymptotic to $4N$ and tends to infinity; it is not $O(N^{-1})$. (e) [Coverage is below nominal in the limit.] $\sqrt{N}\,\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)$ converges in distribution to $\mathcal{N}(0, 8)$, and for every $0 < \alpha < 1$ $\lim_{N \to \infty} \Pr\{|\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) - \tau(d_k, d_l)| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{V}_N}\} = 2\Phi(z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{3/4}) - 1 < 1 - \alpha$ (limit along even $N$). For $\alpha = 0.05$ the limit is $0.9103748944\ldots$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Conditions 1–6, expressions (1), (3), (7), (10), (11) and $\widehat{A_2}$ are transcribed in the standing assumptions, with locations. In this instance $M = 2$ with treatment values written $0, 1$, $K = 2$, $f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i) = z_i$, and $\Omega$ is all of $\{0, 1\}^N$. $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ is the $1 - \alpha/2$ quantile of the standard normal distribution and $\Phi$ its distribution function. The paper does not define $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$ without a hat; the coverage target is $\tau(d_k, d_l)$ (P013-E012, P013-T9).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact for each even $N \ge 4$: the marginal and joint exposure probabilities in (a); the pair score $T_r = 4(Z_a - Z_b)$ with $\Pr(T_r = 0) = 2\epsilon_N$, $\Pr(T_r = 4) = \Pr(T_r = -4) = q_N$, $\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) = N^{-1}\sum_r T_r$ and $\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] = 16nt_N/N^2 = 8t_N/N$; the reduction of (7), (10), (11) to $N^2\widehat{V}_N = \sum_r R_r$ in (b) (the $\widehat{A_2}$ terms vanish, and the only zero joint probabilities in (10) are those with $i = j$); $\mathrm{E}[R_r] = (2\epsilon_N)(2/\epsilon_N) + t_N(16 - 4/t_N) = 16t_N$; $\mathrm{E}[R_r^2] = 8/\epsilon_N + t_N(16 - 4/t_N)^2$; $\Pr(A_N) = t_N^{N/2}$ and $\Pr(A_N^c) \le 1/N$; the closed form for $\mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N)$ in (d). Exact values at $N = 6$ from the validator's enumeration of all 64 assignments: $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau}_6] = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_6) = \mathrm{E}[\widehat{V}_6] = 34/27$, $\Pr(A_6) = 4913/5832$, $6\widehat{V}_6 = 100/17$ on $A_6$, $6\,\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_6) = 68/9$, $\mathrm{Var}(6\widehat{V}_6) = 65536/4131$. The limit statements in (c)–(e) then use $\Pr(A_N^c) \to 0$, the characteristic function $[2\epsilon_N + t_N\cos(4u/\sqrt{N})]^{N/2} \to \exp(-4u^2)$ of $\sqrt{N}\,\widehat{\tau}_N$, and Slutsky's theorem.

The second validator's witness (validate/P013-E001/v2/artifact/derivation.md) is the same family with $\epsilon_n = 1/(4n^3)$. For a sequence at every integer $N$ the validator adds, at odd $N$, one independent Bernoulli$(1/2)$ unit with both potential outcomes equal to 1; failure along even $N$ already refutes the proposition. canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected Proposition 6.2. Changes from the printed statement: (1) one hypothesis, (L) below, is added; (2) the dependency indicator of Condition 5 is the corrected one of P013-T6; (3) the coverage target is $\tau(d_k, d_l)$, in place of the undefined $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$ (P013-T9); (4) the conclusion is a lower limit of the coverage probability, with no claim that the variance ratio or the studentized statistic converges (P013-T8).] [Setting] A sequence of nested finite populations $U_N$, $N \to \infty$. For each $N$: a known design on $U_N$, an exposure mapping, and fixed potential outcomes satisfying Conditions 1 and 2; two distinct exposures $d_k, d_l$ with $0 < \pi_i(d) < 1$ for every $i \in U_N$ and $d \in \{d_k, d_l\}$. Write $\tau_N = \tau(d_k, d_l)$, $\widehat{\tau}_N = \widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)$ of expression (3), $V_N = \mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau}_N]$, and $\widehat{V}_N = \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$ of expression (11), all for the population $U_N$. [Hypotheses] (C3) Condition 3: there are constants $c_1, c_2 < \infty$, not depending on $N$, such that $|y_i(d)| \le c_1$ and $1/\pi_i(d) \le c_2$ for all $N$, all $i \in U_N$ and $d \in \{d_k, d_l\}$. (C5) Condition 5 for a genuine dependency graph: for each $N$ there is a symmetric binary $h_{ij}$, $(i, j) \in U_N \times U_N$, such that for every pair of disjoint sets $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2 \subseteq U_N$ with $h_{ij} = 0$ for all $i \in \Gamma_1$ and $j \in \Gamma_2$, the random vectors $(D_i)_{i \in \Gamma_1}$ and $(D_j)_{j \in \Gamma_2}$ are independent; and there is a finite constant $m$, not depending on $N$, such that $\sum_{j \in U_N} h_{ij} \le m$ for all $N$ and all $i \in U_N$. (C6) Condition 6: $N V_N \to c$, where $c > 0$. (L) [Added] For every $\delta > 0$, $\Pr\{N\widehat{V}_N < N V_N - \delta\} \to 0$. [Conclusion] For every $0 < \alpha < 1$, $\liminf_{N \to \infty} \Pr\{|\widehat{\tau}_N - \tau_N| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{V}_N}\} \ge 1 - \alpha$. [Sufficient conditions for (L), each stated by the validators] (A) $N(\widehat{V}_N - \mathrm{E}[\widehat{V}_N]) \xrightarrow{p} 0$ implies (L), because $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{V}_N] \ge V_N$ (Proposition 5.6); in particular $\mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N) \to 0$ implies (L). (R) Under (C3) and (C5), suppose there is a constant $b > 0$, not depending on $N$, such that every positive joint exposure probability used by (11) is at least $b$: for all $N$ and all $i \ne j$ in $U_N$, each of $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$, $\pi_{ij}(d_l)$ and $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$ is either $0$ or at least $b$. Then $\mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N) = O(N^{-1})$, hence (A) and (L). (R') Under (C3) and (C5), let $b_N$ be the smallest positive value among $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$, $\pi_{ij}(d_l)$, $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$ over $i \ne j$ in $U_N$. Then $\mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N) = O((N b_N)^{-1})$, so $N b_N \to \infty$ implies (A) and (L). [What does not suffice] Conditions 3, 5 and 6 alone, even with the corrected dependency graph, do not imply the conclusion: P013-T1.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 9, the two descriptions of the simulation design's exposure probabilities (the degree-39 student; no no-exposure probability below 0.01), corrected claim
canonical_claim.location: p. 1931 (PDF p. 20); design and exposure mapping on p. 1930 (PDF p. 19)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements: p. 1930 (PDF p. 19)] We simulate experiments in which a treatment, $\mathbf{Z}$, is randomly assigned without replacement and with uniform probability to 1/10 of individuals in a school network. [p. 1931 (PDF p. 20)] [...] with a maximum degree of 39. To give an idea of the range of exposure probabilities, for the student with degree of 39, the probability of isolated direct exposure was 0.00067. [...] About 3% of students have an exposure probability of less than 0.01 for the direct + indirect exposure condition, 0.5% for isolated direct exposure, and then there were no cases with probabilities less than 0.01 for either the indirect- or no-exposure conditions. [Corrected claim, from the validator] Read as probabilities under the stated design, the value 0.00067 for the degree-39 student and the statement that no student has a no-exposure probability below 0.01 are incompatible: at least one of them is inaccurate as a description of design probabilities (they can both hold for finite Monte Carlo estimates of the probabilities, which the section does not say it reports). Which one is inaccurate, and its corrected value, cannot be determined without the school's size and number treated. [Formal content] Let a school have $N$ subjects of whom exactly $n$ are treated, every set of $n$ subjects being equally likely, and let subject $i$ have 39 neighbours in the school, with $1 \le n \le N - 39$. Let $p = \pi_i(d_{10})$ be the probability that $i$ is treated and none of its neighbours is, and $q = \pi_i(d_{00})$ the probability that neither $i$ nor any of its neighbours is treated. (a) $p = \binom{N - 40}{n - 1}\big/\binom{N}{n}$ and $q = \binom{N - 40}{n}\big/\binom{N}{n}$. (b) $q = \frac{N - 39 - n}{n}\,p$. (c) If $N \le 10n + 5$ (which holds when $n = N/10$ and when $n$ is $N/10$ rounded to the nearest integer), then $q \le 9p$. (d) Hence, under (c), $p \le 0.000675$ (every value that rounds to 0.00067 at five decimals satisfies this) implies $q \le 243/40000 = 0.006075 < 0.01$; and $q \ge 1/100$ implies $p \ge 1/900 > 0.000675$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Exposure mapping of Section 9: p. 1930 (PDF p. 19)] $\theta_i$ is a column vector equal to the transpose of subject $i$'s row in a network adjacency matrix (modified such that we have zeroes on the diagonal). The inner product, $\mathbf{z}'\theta_i$, counts the number of subject $i$'s peers assigned to treatment. $f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i) = d_{11}$ (Direct + Indirect Exposure) if $z_i\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i > 0) = 1$; $d_{10}$ (Isolated Direct Exposure) if $z_i\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0) = 1$; $d_{01}$ (Indirect Exposure) if $(1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i > 0) = 1$; $d_{00}$ (No Exposure) if $(1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0) = 1$, where each unit falls into exactly one of the four exposure conditions. Here $z_i \in \{0, 1\}$. [p. 1930] Indirect effects are transmitted only within a subject's school. [p. 1931 (PDF p. 20)] This experiment is repeated independently across the 144 school classes included in Add Health [...]. $\pi_i(d)$ is the exposure probability of the standing assumptions, computed for the design within subject $i$'s school.

canonical_claim.statement: [p. 1922 (PDF p. 11)] LEMMA 5.1. If $\pi_{ij}(d_k) > 0$ for all $i, j$, then $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]] = \mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$. PROPOSITION 5.1. If $\pi_{ij}(d_k) = 0$ for some $i, j$, then $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]] = \mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] + A$, where $A = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U \setminus i : \pi_{ij}(d_k) = 0\}} y_i(d_k)y_j(d_k)$. PROPOSITION 5.2. $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] + \widehat{A_2}(d_k)] \ge \mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$. [Hypotheses: the standing assumptions (a known design, Conditions 1 and 2, $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$) and the convention $0/0 = 0$ in expression (7); Proposition 5.2 carries no further condition and covers both cases.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Expression (7), the convention $0/0 = 0$ and $\widehat{A_2}(d_k)$ are in the standing assumptions (pp. 1921–1922). $\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$ is given by expression (2) (P013-T13). [The general sampling results the paper reproduces, Appendix A.5, pp. 1939–1942 (PDF pp. 28–31), for a population $U$ indexed by $k$ with inclusion indicators $I_k$, $\mathrm{E}(I_k) = \pi_k > 0$, $\mathrm{E}(I_kI_l) = \pi_{kl}$ and $\hat{t} = \sum_{k \in U} I_k y_k/\pi_k$] PROPOSITION A.1. When $s^0$ refers to a sample from a design with some $\pi_{kl} = 0$, we have $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat{t})] = \mathrm{Var}(\hat{t}) + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U \setminus k : \pi_{kl} = 0\}} y_ky_l = \mathrm{Var}(\hat{t}) + A$. [Here, as its proof on p. 1940 writes it for such a design, $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat{t}) = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U : \pi_{kl} > 0\}} I_kI_l \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}$.] Now, consider the following variance estimator: $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}_C}(\hat{t}) = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U : \pi_{kl} > 0\}} I_kI_l \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l} + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U \setminus k : \pi_{kl} = 0\}} \left(I_k\frac{|y_k|^{a_{kl}}}{a_{kl}\pi_k} + I_l\frac{|y_l|^{b_{kl}}}{b_{kl}\pi_l}\right)$, where $a_{kl}, b_{kl}$ are positive real numbers such that $\frac{1}{a_{kl}} + \frac{1}{b_{kl}} = 1$ for all pairs $k, l$ with $\pi_{kl} = 0$. PROPOSITION A.2. $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}_C}(\hat{t})] \ge \mathrm{Var}(\hat{t})$. COROLLARY A.2 [the case $a_{kl} = b_{kl} = 2$, estimator $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}_{C2}}(\hat{t})$]. $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}_{C2}}(\hat{t})] \ge \mathrm{Var}(\hat{t})$.
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-population statements; both readers verified them by exact enumeration on designs with zero joint probabilities and mixed-sign outcomes, and no error touches them. They apply the sampling results of Appendix A.5 with inclusion indicator $\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)$ and value $y_i(d_k)$. With $0/0 = 0$, a pair with $\pi_{ij}(d_k) = 0$ contributes nothing to (7). The inequality behind Proposition 5.2 is Young's inequality with exponents 2: $y_i(d_k)^2/2 + y_j(d_k)^2/2 \ge |y_i(d_k)||y_j(d_k)| \ge -y_i(d_k)y_j(d_k)$, so $A + \mathrm{E}[\widehat{A_2}(d_k)] \ge 0$. The paper also states (p. 1922) that an unbiased estimator for the variance of $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)$ is $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)] = (1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$ under the condition of Lemma 5.1, and defines $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}_A}[\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)] = (1/N^2) [\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] + \widehat{A_2}(d_k)]$.
